title: SYSK Selects: How Miranda Rights Work
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of the episode on how Miranda rights work. Josh introduces it as a favorite. Hosts discuss the cultural ubiquity of the Miranda warning, then the 1966 Miranda v. Arizona case and the four consolidated cases (Vignera v. New York, Westover v. United States, California v. Stewart). They cover Ernesto Miranda's 1963 Phoenix interrogation, the Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination, the distinction between custodial and non-custodial interrogation, traffic stops and implied detention, the fact that unwarned statements can't be used but that failing to read rights doesn't mean release, and the public safety exception from New York v. Quarles (1984), applied in the 2013 Boston bombing suspect's hospital interview and the Times Square bomber case. Closing listener mail discusses a Royal Tenenbaums fan theory about the five stages of grief, and an anniversary shout-out.

segments.title: Selects intro and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh introduces the Selects episode as one of his favorites. Hosts joke about Miranda being a Sex and the City character and about TV cop shows.

segments.title: Miranda warning and the Miranda v. Arizona case
segments.summary: The standard warning is recited and the hosts note its cultural ubiquity. They explain that Miranda v. Arizona (1966) combined four cases, and describe the Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination.

segments.title: Ernesto Miranda's 1963 case and the Supreme Court ruling
segments.summary: Ernesto Miranda was questioned in Phoenix in 1963 about a kidnapping and rape. He was not told he could remain silent and signed a confession. The Supreme Court ruled in 1966 that suspects must be informed of their rights. Miranda was later retried, paroled, sold signed cards, and was stabbed to death in a bar fight; his killer was read his rights and did not talk.

segments.title: Custodial interrogation and when Miranda applies
segments.summary: The ruling hinges on custodial interrogation. Custody means denial of complete freedom of action, which can be implied by police presence. Traffic stops and doorstep questioning are discussed as non-custodial situations where a statement can be used.

segments.title: Consequences of not being read rights
segments.summary: Failing to give Miranda warnings does not mean release. It only bars using the unwarned statement in court and evidence derived from it. Hosts give a hypothetical about admitting to marijuana during a non-custodial stop.

segments.title: Tangent on Mandy Patinkin and Alien Nation
segments.summary: A brief digression about actors and films, including Mandy Patinkin, Alien Nation and Enemy Mine.

segments.title: Public safety exception and the Boston bombing suspect
segments.summary: New York v. Quarles (1984) created a public safety exception allowing questioning before warnings to secure threats such as a loaded gun. The hosts discuss the 2013 hospital interview of the wounded Boston bombing suspect, who confessed before being read his rights, and a judge later ordering warnings. They also mention the Times Square bomber case three years earlier.

segments.title: Debate on rights for terrorism suspects
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the tension between public safety and constitutional rights, saying the public safety exemption suspends rights only for a narrow window of time.

segments.title: Listener mail: Royal Tenenbaums fan theory and anniversary shout-out
segments.summary: A shout-out to a Kentucky teacher couple's anniversary. Listener Josh Bryant offers a fan theory that each Royal Tenenbaums character represents a stage of grief. Hosts respond and ask for fan theories and feral children stories.
